chapters.name: Solid Shore

levels.name: Welcome to the Archipelago
levels.storyContext: Prof. Owlbert welcomes you to the shores of Solid Shore. "Before we explore, we need to know our shapes! 3D solids are all around us."

problems.statement: Which of these is a 3D solid? A) Circle B) Sphere C) Square D) Triangle

correctAnswer.displayValue: B — A sphere is a 3D solid; the others are flat 2D shapes

hints.text: Think about which shape you could hold in your hand like a ball.
2D shapes are flat (circle, square, triangle). 3D shapes have depth.
A sphere is a 3D ball shape. Circles, squares, and triangles are flat.

problems.solutionExplanation: A sphere is a 3D solid — it has depth, unlike flat 2D shapes.
problems.teachingPoint: 3D solids have length, width, and height. 2D shapes are flat — they only have length and width.

problems.statement: A cylinder looks like a soup can. How many flat surfaces does a cylinder have? A) 0 B) 1 C) 2 D) 3

correctAnswer.displayValue: C — A cylinder has 2 flat circular faces (top and bottom) and 1 curved surface

hints.text: Picture a soup can. How many flat parts can it stand on?
A cylinder has a flat top and a flat bottom. The side is curved.
The top circle and the bottom circle are both flat faces. That gives 2.

problems.teachingPoint: A cylinder has 2 flat circular faces and 1 curved surface that wraps around the side.

problems.statement: Match the real-world object to its 3D shape: A basketball is most like a: A) Cube B) Cone C) Sphere D) Cylinder

correctAnswer.displayValue: C — A basketball is shaped like a sphere

hints.text: Think about the shape of a basketball — does it have any flat parts?
A basketball is perfectly round in every direction.
A perfectly round 3D shape with no flat faces is called a sphere.

problems.solutionExplanation: A basketball is a sphere — perfectly round with no flat faces.
problems.teachingPoint: Spheres are perfectly round 3D solids. Every point on the surface is the same distance from the center.

levels.name: Naming the Fleet
levels.storyContext: Lizzie inspects the fleet of ships. "Each ship hull has a different cross-section. Prisms have rectangles, pyramids have triangles!"

problems.statement: A prism has two identical bases connected by rectangular faces. If the bases are triangles, what is the prism called? A) Triangular pyramid B) Triangular prism C) Rectangular prism D) Cone

correctAnswer.displayValue: B — A prism named after its base shape: triangular bases = triangular prism

hints.text: Prisms are named after the shape of their bases.
Triangle bases mean it is a "triangular" something.
Two triangular bases + rectangular sides = triangular prism.

problems.solutionExplanation: Triangular prism — named after its triangular bases.
problems.teachingPoint: Prisms are named by their base shape. A triangular prism has triangular bases; a rectangular prism has rectangular bases.

problems.statement: A pyramid has one base and triangular faces that meet at a point (apex). If the base is a square, what is the pyramid called? A) Triangular pyramid B) Rectangular pyramid C) Square pyramid D) Pentagonal pyramid

correctAnswer.displayValue: C — A square base pyramid is called a square pyramid

hints.text: Pyramids are also named by their base shape.
The base is a square, so the name starts with "square."
Square base + triangular sides meeting at an apex = square pyramid.

problems.solutionExplanation: Square pyramid — named after its square base.
problems.teachingPoint: Pyramids are named by their base shape. A square pyramid has a square base; a triangular pyramid (tetrahedron) has a triangular base.

problems.statement: How is a cylinder different from a prism? A) A cylinder has curved surfaces B) A cylinder has more faces C) A prism has curved surfaces D) They are the same shape

correctAnswer.value: A) A cylinder has curved surfaces
correctAnswer.displayValue: A — A cylinder has a curved lateral surface, while prism faces are all flat

hints.text: Run your hand along a soup can vs a cereal box. What feels different?
One has flat sides (prism) and one has a rounded side.
A cylinder has a curved surface connecting its circular bases. A prism has only flat faces.

problems.solutionExplanation: A cylinder has a curved surface; prisms have only flat rectangular faces.
problems.teachingPoint: Cylinders and prisms both have two identical bases, but cylinders have a curved surface while prisms have flat rectangular faces.

levels.name: Counting Faces
levels.storyContext: Grogg tries counting the sides of a cube. "One... two... wait, did I count that one already?" Let's help him count carefully.

problems.statement: A cube has how many faces?

hints.text: Think of a die — how many numbers can it show?
A cube has a top, bottom, front, back, left, and right face.
Count: top + bottom + front + back + left + right = 6 faces.

problems.solutionExplanation: 6 faces — top, bottom, front, back, left, right
problems.teachingPoint: A cube has 6 square faces. Each face is identical in size and shape.

problems.statement: A triangular prism has how many faces? (Count both triangular bases and rectangular sides.)

hints.text: A triangular prism has triangular bases and rectangular sides.
It has 2 triangular bases. How many rectangles connect them?
A triangle has 3 sides, so 3 rectangles connect the bases. Total: 2 + 3 = 5.

problems.teachingPoint: A triangular prism has 5 faces: 2 triangular bases and 3 rectangular lateral faces.

problems.statement: A square pyramid has how many faces in total? (Count the base and all the triangular sides.)

hints.text: A square pyramid has a square base and triangular sides.
The square base has 4 edges. Each edge has a triangle above it.
1 square base + 4 triangular faces = 5 faces total.

problems.teachingPoint: A pyramid with an n-sided base has n + 1 faces: 1 base + n triangular sides.

levels.name: Edges and Vertices
levels.storyContext: Lizzie traces the edges of each solid with her finger. "An edge is where two faces meet. A vertex is a corner point."

problems.statement: A cube has how many edges? (An edge is a line segment where two faces meet.)

hints.text: Think about the top face — it has 4 edges. But edges are shared.
A cube has 4 edges on top, 4 on bottom, and 4 vertical edges connecting them.
Top edges: 4, bottom edges: 4, vertical edges: 4. Total = 12.

problems.solutionExplanation: 12 edges: 4 on top + 4 on bottom + 4 vertical
problems.teachingPoint: A cube has 12 edges. Edges are line segments where two faces meet.

problems.statement: A cube has how many vertices? (A vertex is a corner point where edges meet.)

hints.text: Vertices are corner points. How many corners does a box have?
The top face has 4 corners. The bottom face has 4 corners.
4 corners on top + 4 corners on bottom = 8 vertices.

problems.teachingPoint: A cube has 8 vertices. A vertex is a point where three or more edges meet.

problems.statement: A triangular pyramid (tetrahedron) has 4 triangular faces. How many vertices does it have?

hints.text: A triangular pyramid has a triangular base and an apex point above it.
The base triangle has 3 corners. Plus the apex point on top.
3 base vertices + 1 apex vertex = 4 vertices total.

problems.teachingPoint: A tetrahedron has 4 vertices, 6 edges, and 4 triangular faces. It is the simplest 3D solid with all flat faces.

levels.name: Euler's Discovery
levels.storyContext: Prof. Owlbert pulls out an ancient scroll. "The great mathematician Euler found a pattern connecting vertices, edges, and faces of every solid!"

problems.statement: A cube has V=8 vertices, E=12 edges, F=6 faces. Calculate V - E + F.

hints.text: Substitute the values: V=8, E=12, F=6 into V - E + F.
Calculate step by step: first 8 - 12 = -4, then -4 + 6 = ?

problems.teachingPoint: Euler's formula states that for any convex polyhedron, V - E + F = 2. This works for every solid with flat faces!

problems.statement: A triangular prism has V=6, E=9, F=5. What is V - E + F?

hints.text: Substitute V=6, E=9, F=5 into the formula V - E + F.
6 - 9 + 5 = -3 + 5 = 2. The same result as the cube!

problems.solutionExplanation: V - E + F = 6 - 9 + 5 = 2 — same as the cube!
problems.teachingPoint: This is Euler's formula: V - E + F always equals 2 for convex polyhedra. It works for cubes, prisms, pyramids, and more!

problems.statement: A square pyramid has V=5, E=8. Using Euler's formula V - E + F = 2, how many faces does a square pyramid have?

hints.text: Use Euler's formula: V - E + F = 2. You know V and E — solve for F.
F = 2 - 5 + 8 = 5. A square pyramid has 5 faces.

problems.teachingPoint: Euler's formula can predict any one of V, E, or F if you know the other two. It is a powerful tool for checking your work!

levels.name: Testing Euler's Formula
levels.storyContext: Grogg wants to test the formula on every shape he can find. "Let me check — does it REALLY always work?"

problems.statement: A pentagonal prism has 7 faces and 10 vertices. Using V - E + F = 2, how many edges does it have?

hints.text: Rearrange Euler's formula to solve for E: E = V + F - 2.

problems.teachingPoint: You can rearrange Euler's formula to find any missing value: E = V + F - 2.

problems.statement: A hexagonal pyramid has 7 vertices and 12 edges. How many faces does it have?

hints.text: Use Euler's formula: V - E + F = 2, and solve for F.

problems.solutionExplanation: F = 7 faces: 1 hexagonal base + 6 triangular sides
problems.teachingPoint: A hexagonal pyramid has 7 faces. Euler's formula confirms: 7 - 12 + 7 = 2. It checks out!

problems.statement: An octahedron has 6 vertices and 8 faces. How many edges does it have?

hints.text: Apply Euler's formula: E = V + F - 2.

problems.teachingPoint: An octahedron (8 triangular faces) has 12 edges and 6 vertices. Euler's formula: 6 - 12 + 8 = 2.

levels.name: Slicing Solids
levels.storyContext: Lizzie picks up a clay cube and slices it with a wire. "Look — the shape where I cut is called a cross-section!"

problems.statement: If you slice a cube straight across parallel to one face, what shape is the cross-section? A) Triangle B) Square C) Circle D) Pentagon

correctAnswer.displayValue: B — Slicing a cube parallel to a face creates a square cross-section

hints.text: Imagine cutting a block of cheese straight across. What shape is the flat cut?
If you cut parallel to one of the square faces, the cross-section matches that face.
Cutting parallel to a square face of a cube gives a square cross-section.

problems.solutionExplanation: A square cross-section — cutting parallel to a face gives that face shape.
problems.teachingPoint: A cross-section is the shape you get when you slice through a 3D solid. Cutting parallel to a face gives a cross-section that matches the face.

problems.statement: If you slice a cylinder horizontally (parallel to its circular base), what shape is the cross-section? A) Rectangle B) Oval C) Circle D) Triangle

correctAnswer.displayValue: C — Slicing a cylinder parallel to its base gives a circle

hints.text: Think about cutting a can of soup sideways. What shape is the cut?
The base of a cylinder is circular. A parallel cut matches the base shape.
Cutting parallel to the circular base gives a circle cross-section.

problems.solutionExplanation: A circle — parallel to the circular base.
problems.teachingPoint: Slicing a cylinder parallel to its base always produces a circle. Slicing vertically through the center produces a rectangle.

problems.statement: If you slice a cone horizontally (parallel to its base), what shape is the cross-section? A) Triangle B) Circle C) Square D) Oval

correctAnswer.displayValue: B — A horizontal slice of a cone gives a smaller circle

hints.text: Think about what happens if you cut an ice cream cone sideways.
The base of a cone is a circle. A parallel cut should be a similar shape.
A horizontal slice of a cone gives a smaller circle than the base.

problems.solutionExplanation: A circle — smaller than the base. Higher cuts give smaller circles.
problems.teachingPoint: A horizontal cross-section of a cone is always a circle. The higher you cut, the smaller the circle.

levels.name: Cross-Section Challenge
levels.storyContext: Admiral Axiom appears. "Can you figure out the TRICKY cross-sections? Not all slices are straight across!"

problems.statement: If you slice a cube diagonally from one edge to the opposite edge, what shape could the cross-section be? A) Only a square B) Only a triangle C) A rectangle or triangle D) A hexagon

correctAnswer.displayValue: C — Diagonal slices of a cube can produce rectangles or triangles depending on angle

hints.text: Imagine cutting from a top edge to the opposite bottom edge at an angle.
A diagonal cut through a corner can create a triangle. Other angles create rectangles.
Cutting corner to corner gives a triangle; cutting edge to opposite edge gives a rectangle.

problems.solutionExplanation: Diagonal cuts can produce rectangles or triangles depending on the angle.
problems.teachingPoint: A single solid can have many different cross-section shapes depending on the angle and position of the cut.

problems.statement: Which cross-section is IMPOSSIBLE to make by slicing a cube? A) Triangle B) Rectangle C) Pentagon D) Circle

correctAnswer.displayValue: D — You cannot create a circular cross-section from a cube (all cube faces are flat and straight)

hints.text: Think about what shapes a straight cut through flat surfaces can make.
Cubes have only flat, straight edges. Can a straight cut make a curved shape?
A circle is curved, but all cube cross-sections have straight edges. Circles are impossible.

problems.solutionExplanation: A circle — impossible because cube faces are flat, so cross-sections have straight edges.
problems.teachingPoint: Cross-sections of polyhedra (flat-faced solids) always have straight edges. You can never get a circle from slicing a cube!

problems.statement: If you slice a cylinder vertically through its center (perpendicular to the base), what shape is the cross-section? A) Circle B) Rectangle C) Triangle D) Oval

correctAnswer.displayValue: B — A vertical slice through a cylinder gives a rectangle

hints.text: Imagine cutting a soup can straight down through the middle.
The height of the cylinder becomes one side, the diameter becomes the other.
The cross-section is a rectangle with width = diameter and height = cylinder height.

problems.solutionExplanation: A rectangle with width equal to the diameter and height equal to the cylinder height.
problems.teachingPoint: Different orientations of the same cut produce different cross-sections. Horizontal cuts of a cylinder give circles; vertical cuts give rectangles.

levels.name: Unfolding Shapes
levels.storyContext: Grogg finds a flattened cardboard box. "If I unfold a 3D shape flat, that pattern is called a NET!"

problems.statement: A cube has 6 square faces. When you unfold a cube into a net, how many squares will the net have? A) 4 B) 5 C) 6 D) 8

correctAnswer.displayValue: C — A cube net has exactly 6 squares, one for each face

hints.text: Each face of the cube becomes one shape in the net.
A cube has 6 faces, so its net needs exactly 6 squares.
A cube has 6 faces → the net has 6 squares arranged so they fold back into a cube.

problems.solutionExplanation: 6 squares — one for each face of the cube.
problems.teachingPoint: A net is a 2D pattern that folds into a 3D shape. The number of shapes in the net equals the number of faces.

problems.statement: A net is a cross-shaped arrangement of 6 squares. Can this fold into a cube? A) Yes B) No

correctAnswer.displayValue: A — The cross shape is one of 11 possible nets for a cube

hints.text: Imagine folding each square up from the center square.
The center is the bottom, the four arms fold up as sides, and one arm becomes the top.
A cross of 6 squares folds into a cube. The center becomes one face, and 4 sides fold up plus 1 top.

problems.solutionExplanation: Yes — the cross is a valid cube net.
problems.teachingPoint: There are exactly 11 different nets that fold into a cube. The cross shape is the most recognizable one.

problems.statement: A rectangular prism (box) has 6 rectangular faces. When you unfold it, how many rectangles are in its net?

hints.text: Just like a cube, each face becomes one shape in the net.
A rectangular prism has 6 faces (3 pairs of matching rectangles).
The net has 6 rectangles: top, bottom, front, back, left, right.

problems.solutionExplanation: 6 rectangles — one for each face of the rectangular prism.
problems.teachingPoint: A rectangular prism net has 6 rectangles: 3 pairs of identical rectangles (top/bottom, front/back, left/right).

levels.name: Net Detective
levels.storyContext: Lizzie lays out flat patterns. "Which ones actually fold into 3D shapes? Some are tricky impostors!"

problems.statement: A net has 6 squares arranged in a straight line (1×6 strip). Can this fold into a cube? A) Yes B) No

correctAnswer.displayValue: B — A straight line of 6 squares cannot fold into a cube because squares would overlap

hints.text: Try to imagine folding a strip of 6 squares into a box shape.
When you fold a straight strip, the 5th and 6th squares would overlap earlier ones.
A 1×6 strip is NOT a valid cube net. Two squares would need to be on the same face.

problems.solutionExplanation: No — a straight line of 6 squares overlaps when folded, so it is not a valid cube net.
problems.teachingPoint: Not every arrangement of 6 squares is a valid cube net. The squares must be arranged so no two overlap when folded.

problems.statement: A T-shape made of 6 squares (3 in a row on top, 3 going down from the middle) — can this fold into a cube? A) Yes B) No

correctAnswer.displayValue: A — The T-shape is one of the 11 valid cube nets

hints.text: Imagine the bottom of the T as the base, then fold the arms up.
The bottom 3 squares fold up as front, bottom, and back. The top 2 become sides, and 1 becomes top.
The T-shape is a valid cube net — it is one of exactly 11 arrangements that work.

problems.solutionExplanation: Yes — the T-shape is a valid cube net.
problems.teachingPoint: Of the 35 possible arrangements of 6 connected squares, exactly 11 are valid cube nets. The T-shape is one of them.

problems.statement: There are exactly how many different nets that can fold into a cube?

hints.text: This is a famous result in geometry. It is more than 5 but less than 20.
Mathematicians have proven the exact number. It is a two-digit number starting with 1.
There are exactly 11 distinct nets that fold into a cube.

problems.solutionExplanation: 11 distinct cube nets — verified by systematic enumeration.
problems.teachingPoint: There are exactly 11 different nets that fold into a cube. This was proven by systematically checking all possible arrangements of 6 connected squares.

levels.name: Surface Area Foundations
levels.storyContext: Prof. Owlbert explains: "Surface area is the total area of all the faces. Imagine painting every outside surface of the shape!"

problems.statement: A cube has 6 faces, each a square with side length 3 cm. What is the area of ONE face in square cm?

hints.text: The area of a square is side × side.
Each face is a 3 cm × 3 cm square.

problems.solutionExplanation: 9 sq cm — area of a 3 cm × 3 cm square face
problems.teachingPoint: The area of a square is side × side (or side²). For a 3 cm square, the area is 3² = 9 sq cm.

problems.statement: A cube has 6 faces, each with area 9 sq cm. What is the total surface area of the cube in square cm?

hints.text: Surface area = sum of all face areas.
All 6 faces are identical, so multiply one face area by 6.
6 faces × 9 sq cm = 54 sq cm total surface area.

problems.teachingPoint: For a cube with side length s, the surface area is 6s². Here: 6 × 3² = 6 × 9 = 54 sq cm.

problems.statement: A rectangular prism is 4 cm long, 3 cm wide, and 2 cm tall. What is its total surface area in square cm? (Hint: find the area of each pair of faces.)

hints.text: A rectangular prism has 3 pairs of identical faces: top/bottom, front/back, left/right.
Top/bottom: 4×3. Front/back: 4×2. Left/right: 3×2. Each pair has 2 faces.

problems.teachingPoint: Surface area of a rectangular prism = 2(lw + lh + wh). Multiply each pair of dimensions and double them since each face appears twice.

levels.name: Surface Area Workshop
levels.storyContext: Admiral Axiom challenges: "Can you handle surface area when the shapes get tricky?"

problems.statement: A cube has a surface area of 150 sq cm. What is the side length of the cube in cm?

hints.text: Surface area of a cube = 6 × (side)². Work backwards from 150.

problems.teachingPoint: To find the side length from surface area: divide by 6, then take the square root. SA/6 = s², so s = √(SA/6).

problems.statement: Rectangular prism A is 5×5×2. Prism B is 4×4×4. Without fully calculating, which has the greater surface area? Enter A or B.

correctAnswer.displayValue: B has SA = 96; A has SA = 90. The cube has greater surface area.

hints.text: Think about how "spread out" each shape is versus being compact like a cube.

problems.solutionExplanation: A has SA = 90, B has SA = 96. B has the greater surface area.
problems.teachingPoint: A cube has the least surface area for a given volume among rectangular prisms, but it can still have more surface area than a flatter shape with less volume.

problems.statement: A rectangular prism is 6 cm × 4 cm × 3 cm. What is its total surface area in square cm?

hints.text: Find the three different face areas, then sum and double.

problems.teachingPoint: Surface area of a rectangular prism: add the three different face areas and multiply by 2. SA = 2(lw + lh + wh).

levels.name: Guardian of Solid Shore
levels.storyContext: The Guardian of Solid Shore rises from the rocks! "Prove your mastery of 3D solids — Euler's formula, cross-sections, and surface area!"

problems.statement: A solid has 20 triangular faces and 12 vertices. Using Euler's formula V - E + F = 2, how many edges does it have?

hints.text: Apply Euler's formula: V - E + F = 2. You know V and F.

problems.teachingPoint: This is an icosahedron — one of the five Platonic solids. Euler's formula works for all convex polyhedra.

problems.statement: You slice a cube at an angle through 6 edges (one on each face). What shape is the cross-section? A) Triangle B) Square C) Hexagon D) Circle

correctAnswer.displayValue: C — Slicing through all 6 faces at an angle creates a hexagonal cross-section

hints.text: If the slice passes through all 6 faces, the cross-section has 6 sides.
Each face contributes one edge to the cross-section. 6 faces = 6 edges.
A slice through all 6 faces of a cube creates a regular hexagon at the right angle.

problems.solutionExplanation: A hexagon — 6 faces means 6 edges in the cross-section.
problems.teachingPoint: A cross-section of a cube that passes through all 6 faces creates a hexagon. At the right angle, it is a regular hexagon!

problems.statement: A cube has a surface area of 216 sq cm. What is the volume of the cube in cubic cm? (Volume = side × side × side)

hints.text: First find the side length from the surface area, then compute volume.
6s² = 216, so s² = 36, s = 6. Now find s³.

problems.teachingPoint: To go from surface area to volume: find s from SA = 6s², then compute V = s³. Here the surface area and volume happen to be the same number!

learningObjectives: Identify 3D solids: prisms, pyramids, cylinders, cones, spheres
Count faces, edges, and vertices of polyhedra
Apply Euler's formula V - E + F = 2
Determine cross-sections of 3D solids
Identify and analyze nets of cubes and prisms
Calculate surface area of cubes and rectangular prisms

chapters.name: Integer Isles

levels.name: Below Zero
levels.storyContext: Grogg shivers on Integer Isles. "Brrr! The temperature is -5°C! What does a negative number even mean?"

problems.statement: The temperature is -5°C. Is this above or below freezing (0°C)? A) Above freezing B) Below freezing C) At freezing

correctAnswer.displayValue: B — Negative numbers are below zero

hints.text: What does the minus sign in front of 5 tell you?
Negative numbers are less than zero. Freezing is 0°C.
-5°C is 5 degrees below zero, so it is below freezing.

problems.solutionExplanation: Below freezing — negative numbers are less than zero.
problems.teachingPoint: Negative numbers represent values less than zero. They are used for temperatures below freezing, depths below sea level, and debts.

problems.statement: A submarine is at -200 meters (200 meters below sea level). A bird is at +50 meters. Who is higher? A) The submarine B) The bird C) They are at the same height

correctAnswer.displayValue: B — +50 meters is higher than -200 meters

hints.text: Positive means above sea level. Negative means below sea level.
+50 is above the surface. -200 is deep underwater.
The bird at +50m is 250 meters above the submarine at -200m.

problems.solutionExplanation: The bird at +50m is higher than the submarine at -200m.
problems.teachingPoint: Positive numbers represent positions above a reference point (like sea level). Negative numbers represent positions below it.

problems.statement: Which of these represents a $15 debt? A) +15 B) -15 C) 0 D) 15

correctAnswer.displayValue: B — Debts are represented by negative numbers

hints.text: A debt means you owe money — it is money you do not have.
Debts are like being "below zero" in your bank account.
A $15 debt is represented as -15 because it is 15 below zero.

problems.teachingPoint: In real life, negative numbers represent debts, losses, or decreases. A balance of -15 means you owe $15.

levels.name: The Number Line Dock
levels.storyContext: Lizzie draws a number line on the dock. "Zero is in the middle. Positive numbers go right, negative numbers go left."

problems.statement: On a number line, which direction do negative numbers go? A) Right B) Left C) Up D) Down

correctAnswer.displayValue: B — Negative numbers go to the left of zero on a number line

hints.text: Think about where zero is and which side has smaller numbers.
Numbers decrease as you move left. Negative numbers are less than zero.
On a horizontal number line, negatives are to the LEFT of zero.

problems.solutionExplanation: Left — negative numbers are to the left of zero.
problems.teachingPoint: On a horizontal number line, numbers increase to the right and decrease to the left. Negative numbers are always to the left of zero.

problems.statement: Place these numbers in order from least to greatest: 3, -7, 0, -2, 5. Which comes first (is least)? A) 3 B) -7 C) 0 D) -2

correctAnswer.displayValue: B — On a number line, -7 is farthest to the left, so it is the least

hints.text: The least number is farthest to the left on the number line.
Compare the negative numbers: -7 is farther from zero than -2.

problems.teachingPoint: When ordering integers, more negative means smaller. -7 < -2 < 0 < 3 < 5.

problems.statement: Which number is farther from zero on the number line: -8 or 6? A) -8 B) 6 C) They are the same distance

correctAnswer.displayValue: A — The distance from zero to -8 is 8 units, while 6 is only 6 units from zero

hints.text: Distance from zero ignores the sign — just look at how far each is from 0.
-8 is 8 units from zero. 6 is 6 units from zero.
8 > 6, so -8 is farther from zero than 6 is.

problems.solutionExplanation: -8 is 8 units from zero; 6 is 6 units from zero. -8 is farther.
problems.teachingPoint: Distance from zero is called absolute value. |-8| = 8 and |6| = 6. Since 8 > 6, -8 is farther from zero.

levels.name: Distance from Zero
levels.storyContext: Prof. Owlbert introduces a new symbol. "The absolute value bars |x| mean the distance from zero. Distance is always positive!"

problems.statement: What is the absolute value of -9? (Write just the number.)

hints.text: Absolute value is the distance from zero — it drops the negative sign.
-9 is 9 units away from zero on the number line.
|-9| = 9. The distance from zero to -9 is 9 units.

problems.teachingPoint: Absolute value |x| is the distance from x to zero. It is always non-negative. |-9| = 9 and |9| = 9.

problems.statement: What is |7| + |-3|?

hints.text: Find each absolute value first, then add.

problems.teachingPoint: Compute each absolute value separately, then perform the operation. |7| = 7, |-3| = 3, so the sum is 10.

problems.statement: True or false: |-5| = |5|. A) True B) False

correctAnswer.displayValue: A — Both are 5 units from zero, so both absolute values are 5

hints.text: Absolute value measures distance from zero, regardless of direction.
-5 is 5 units left of zero; 5 is 5 units right. Same distance.

problems.solutionExplanation: True — both are 5 units from zero.
problems.teachingPoint: A number and its opposite always have the same absolute value. |-a| = |a| for any number a.

levels.name: Comparing Integers
levels.storyContext: Grogg lines up integers on the dock. "Is -3 greater than -7? This is confusing!" Let's compare carefully.

problems.statement: Which is greater: -3 or -7? A) -3 B) -7 C) They are equal

correctAnswer.displayValue: A — On a number line, -3 is to the right of -7, so -3 > -7

hints.text: Think about temperature: -3°C or -7°C — which is warmer?
-3 is closer to zero than -7. Closer to zero means greater.
-3 > -7 because -3 is to the right of -7 on the number line.

problems.solutionExplanation: -3 > -7. Farther left on the number line means smaller.
problems.teachingPoint: For negative numbers, the one closer to zero is greater. -3 > -7 because -3 is only 3 units from zero while -7 is 7 units away.

problems.statement: Put the correct symbol (<, >, or =) between these numbers: -4 ___ 2

correctAnswer.displayValue: -4 < 2 — any negative is less than any positive

hints.text: Is a negative number ever greater than a positive number?
All negative numbers are to the left of all positive numbers on the number line.
-4 < 2. Every negative number is less than every positive number.

problems.teachingPoint: Every negative number is less than every positive number. The number line shows: all negatives are left of zero, all positives are right.

problems.statement: Order these integers from least to greatest, separated by commas: 4, -1, -6, 0, 2

hints.text: Start with the most negative number and work towards the most positive.
The negatives come first: -6, then -1, then 0, then the positives.

problems.teachingPoint: To order integers: start with the most negative (farthest left on the number line) and go right to the most positive.

levels.name: Adding Same Signs
levels.storyContext: Prof. Owlbert explains: "When you add two positive numbers OR two negative numbers, just add and keep the sign!"

hints.text: Both numbers are negative, so the sum is also negative.
Add the absolute values: 3 + 5 = 8. Then make it negative.

problems.teachingPoint: When adding two negatives, add their absolute values and keep the negative sign. (-3) + (-5) = -(3+5) = -8.

hints.text: Same sign addition: add the values, keep the sign.
7 + 4 = 11. Both are negative, so the answer is negative.

problems.teachingPoint: Same sign rule: add the absolute values and keep the common sign. Two negatives added give a more negative result.

hints.text: Two negative numbers added together — the result is negative.

problems.teachingPoint: Adding two negatives always gives a more negative number. Think of it as going further left on the number line.

levels.name: Adding Different Signs
levels.storyContext: Lizzie explains: "When one number is positive and one is negative, subtract and keep the sign of the bigger absolute value."

problems.statement: What is 8 + (-3)?

hints.text: Positive and negative: subtract the smaller from the larger absolute value.
|8| = 8 > |-3| = 3. Subtract: 8 - 3 = 5. The larger is positive, so the answer is positive.

problems.teachingPoint: Different signs: subtract the smaller absolute value from the larger one. The result takes the sign of the number with the larger absolute value.

problems.statement: What is (-10) + 4?

hints.text: Different signs: subtract the absolute values and keep the sign of the bigger one.

problems.teachingPoint: Since |-10| > |4|, the answer takes the negative sign. 10 - 4 = 6, so the result is -6.

problems.statement: What is (-6) + 6?

hints.text: What happens when you add a number and its opposite?
(-6) + 6 = 0. A number plus its opposite always equals zero.

problems.teachingPoint: A number and its opposite are called additive inverses. They always sum to zero: a + (-a) = 0.

levels.name: Integer Addition Practice
levels.storyContext: Grogg practices adding integers on the dock. "I'm getting the hang of this — positive plus negative, negative plus negative!"

problems.statement: What is (-15) + 9?

hints.text: Different signs: subtract the smaller absolute value from the larger.

problems.teachingPoint: When adding integers with different signs, subtract the absolute values and use the sign of the number with the greater absolute value.

problems.statement: What is 7 + (-11)?

hints.text: Different signs: which has the larger absolute value?

problems.teachingPoint: The negative number has the larger absolute value (11 > 7), so the result is negative: -(11-7) = -4.

problems.statement: A diver is at -30 meters. She rises 12 meters. What is her new depth in meters?

hints.text: Rising means adding a positive number to her depth.
-30 + 12: different signs, subtract: 30 - 12 = 18. Negative is larger.

problems.teachingPoint: Word problems with integers: "rises" means add positive, "descends" means add negative. -30 + 12 = -18 meters.

levels.name: Subtraction Secret
levels.storyContext: Prof. Owlbert reveals: "Here is the big secret of integer subtraction: subtracting is the SAME as adding the opposite!"

problems.statement: What is 5 - 8? (Rewrite as 5 + (-8) first.)

hints.text: Subtracting 8 is the same as adding -8.

problems.teachingPoint: Subtracting a number is the same as adding its opposite: a - b = a + (-b). This rule makes all subtraction into addition!

problems.statement: What is (-3) - 7?

hints.text: Now it is two negatives: 3 + 7 = 10, result is negative.

problems.teachingPoint: Convert to addition: (-3) - 7 = (-3) + (-7). Now apply same-sign addition: -(3+7) = -10.

hints.text: Subtracting a negative is the same as adding a positive!

problems.teachingPoint: Subtracting a negative = adding a positive: a - (-b) = a + b. Two negatives make a positive!

levels.name: Integer Subtraction Workshop
levels.storyContext: Lizzie sets up a workshop. "Practice makes perfect. Remember: always rewrite subtraction as adding the opposite!"

problems.statement: What is 3 - (-5)?

hints.text: Subtracting a negative means adding a positive.

problems.teachingPoint: Remember: subtracting a negative is the same as adding. 3 - (-5) = 3 + 5 = 8.

hints.text: Different signs: 8 - 3 = 5. The negative has larger absolute value.

problems.teachingPoint: Step 1: Rewrite as addition of opposite. Step 2: Apply integer addition rules.

problems.statement: The temperature was -6°C in the morning and dropped 8 more degrees by night. What is the nighttime temperature?

hints.text: "Dropped 8 degrees" means subtract 8 from the morning temperature.
-6 - 8 = -6 + (-8). Two negatives: add and keep negative.

problems.teachingPoint: "Dropping" temperature means subtracting. -6 - 8 = -6 + (-8) = -14°C. The temperature got even colder.

levels.name: Grogg's Integer Errors
levels.storyContext: Grogg shows his work. "I think I got these right!" Can you spot his mistakes?

problems.statement: Grogg says: "(-5) + (-3) = 2 because the negatives cancel out." What is the correct answer? A) 2 B) -2 C) 8 D) -8

correctAnswer.displayValue: D — Two negatives add to a more negative result: (-5)+(-3) = -8

hints.text: Do negatives "cancel out" when you add two negative numbers?
Adding two negatives makes a MORE negative number, not positive.
(-5) + (-3) = -(5+3) = -8. Grogg confused addition with subtraction rules.

problems.solutionExplanation: (-5) + (-3) = -8. Negatives only "cancel" when you add a positive and negative.
problems.teachingPoint: Common error: Two negatives do NOT cancel when adding. They cancel when multiplying. (-5)+(-3) = -8, not +2.

problems.statement: Grogg says: "7 - (-2) = 5 because 7 minus 2 is 5." What is the correct answer? A) 5 B) 9 C) -5 D) -9

correctAnswer.displayValue: B — Subtracting a negative means adding: 7-(-2) = 7+2 = 9

hints.text: What does subtracting a negative really mean?
Subtracting -2 is the same as adding +2.
7 - (-2) = 7 + 2 = 9. Grogg forgot to change the sign.

problems.teachingPoint: Subtracting a negative = adding a positive. 7 - (-2) = 7 + 2 = 9. The two minus signs combine to make a plus.

problems.statement: Grogg says: "|-4| = -4 because the number is negative." What is the correct value of |-4|? A) -4 B) 4 C) 0 D) -8

correctAnswer.displayValue: B — Absolute value is always non-negative: |-4| = 4

hints.text: Absolute value measures distance. Can distance be negative?
Absolute value strips away the sign and gives a positive result.

problems.teachingPoint: Absolute value is always ≥ 0. It measures distance from zero, and distance cannot be negative. |x| ≥ 0 for all x.

levels.name: Elevation Explorer
levels.storyContext: The crew explores different islands. "Each island has different elevations — some above sea level, some below!"

problems.statement: A mountain peak is at 120 meters above sea level (+120). A cave entrance is at 35 meters below sea level (-35). What is the difference in elevation between the peak and cave?

hints.text: Difference means subtract: peak elevation - cave elevation.
120 - (-35) = 120 + 35 because subtracting a negative is adding.

problems.teachingPoint: To find the difference between two elevations (one above, one below sea level), subtract: the result is the total vertical distance between them.

problems.statement: A bank account has $45. A debit of $60 is made. What is the new balance?

hints.text: A debit means money is taken out — subtract from the balance.
45 - 60: the debit is more than the balance, so the result is negative.

problems.teachingPoint: When you spend more than you have, the balance goes negative. This represents a debt or overdraft.

problems.statement: At 6 AM the temperature is -8°C. By noon it warms up by 15 degrees. What is the noon temperature?

hints.text: "Warms up by 15" means add 15 to the current temperature.
-8 + 15 = 7°C. The temperature is now above freezing!

problems.teachingPoint: Integer addition in context: warming up means adding a positive number. -8 + 15 = 7°C means the temperature crossed zero and went positive.

levels.name: Integer Puzzles
levels.storyContext: Admiral Axiom presents puzzles. "Find the missing integers! Work backwards from the clues."

problems.statement: I think of an integer, add 7, and get 3. What was my integer?

hints.text: Work backwards: if adding 7 gives 3, what was the starting number?

problems.teachingPoint: To work backwards, do the opposite operation. If x + 7 = 3, then x = 3 - 7 = -4.

problems.statement: I think of an integer, subtract 5, and get -9. What was my integer?

hints.text: If subtracting 5 gives -9, undo by adding 5.

problems.teachingPoint: Undo subtraction with addition: if x - 5 = -9, then x = -9 + 5 = -4.

problems.statement: The sum of two integers is -3. One of the integers is 8. What is the other integer?

hints.text: If 8 + x = -3, solve for x by subtracting 8 from both sides.

problems.teachingPoint: To find a missing addend: other = sum - known. -3 - 8 = -11.

levels.name: Guardian of Integer Isles
levels.storyContext: The Guardian of Integer Isles blocks your path! "Show me you truly understand positive, negative, and everything in between!"

hints.text: First convert all subtractions to adding the opposite.

problems.teachingPoint: For long expressions with integers, convert all subtractions to additions, then group positives and negatives separately before combining.

problems.statement: An elevator starts at floor -2, goes up 7 floors, then down 4 floors, then up 3 floors. What floor is it on now?

hints.text: Track each move: start at -2, then add or subtract for each move.

problems.teachingPoint: Track sequences of movements by chaining additions and subtractions. Up = add, down = subtract.

hints.text: Evaluate inside the absolute value bars first, then take absolute values.

problems.teachingPoint: When absolute values contain expressions, evaluate the expression first, then take the absolute value. Work from the inside out.

learningObjectives: Understand negative numbers in real-world contexts
Place and order integers on a number line
Find absolute value of integers
Add integers with same and different signs
Subtract integers using the additive inverse
Solve word problems involving integers

chapters.name: Expression Expanse

levels.name: Letters for Numbers
levels.storyContext: Prof. Owlbert explains: "In algebra, we use letters to stand for unknown numbers. The letter n could be any number!"

problems.statement: If n stands for a number and n + 5 = 12, what is n? A) 5 B) 7 C) 12 D) 17
problems.teachingPoint: A variable is a letter that represents an unknown number. We can find its value by using inverse operations.

problems.statement: If x = 4, what is 3x? (3x means 3 times x)

hints.text: 3x means 3 multiplied by x. Substitute x = 4.

problems.teachingPoint: When a number is written right next to a variable (like 3x), it means multiplication. 3x = 3 × x.

problems.statement: If y = 10, what is y - 3?
problems.teachingPoint: To evaluate an expression, replace the variable with its value and compute. If y = 10, then y - 3 = 10 - 3 = 7.

levels.name: Writing Expressions
levels.storyContext: Lizzie translates words into math. "'Five more than a number' becomes n + 5. Let's practice!"

problems.statement: Write an expression for "a number n increased by 8". Use n as the variable.

hints.text: Start with the variable n and add 8.

problems.teachingPoint: "Increased by," "more than," and "plus" all mean addition. "A number n increased by 8" translates to n + 8.

problems.statement: Write an expression for "twice a number n." Use n as the variable.
problems.teachingPoint: "Twice," "double," and "two times" all mean multiply by 2. In algebra, we write 2n instead of 2 × n.

problems.statement: Write an expression for "7 less than a number n."

hints.text: "Less than" means subtraction, but watch the order carefully.
"7 less than n" means start with n and take away 7.
"7 less than n" = n - 7. Be careful: it is NOT 7 - n!

problems.teachingPoint: "7 less than n" = n - 7 (NOT 7 - n). The "less than" phrase reverses the order — start with the number, then subtract.

levels.name: Plugging In
levels.storyContext: Grogg substitutes values into expressions. "Just replace the letter with the number and calculate!"

problems.statement: If n = 6, what is 4n + 3?

hints.text: Replace n with 6 and follow order of operations.

problems.teachingPoint: When evaluating expressions, do multiplication before addition (order of operations). 4n + 3 = 4×6 + 3 = 27.

problems.statement: If a = 5 and b = 3, what is 2a + b?

hints.text: Replace a with 5 and b with 3.

problems.teachingPoint: Expressions can have multiple variables. Replace each variable with its value and compute using order of operations.

problems.statement: If x = 8, what is (x + 2) × 3?

hints.text: Replace x with 8, then follow order of operations (parentheses first!).

problems.teachingPoint: Parentheses change the order! (x + 2) × 3 means add first, then multiply. Without parentheses, x + 2 × 3 would multiply first.

levels.name: Order of Operations
levels.storyContext: Prof. Owlbert writes PEMDAS on the board. "Parentheses, Exponents, Multiplication/Division, Addition/Subtraction — always in this order!"

problems.statement: What is 3 + 4 × 2? (Remember: multiplication before addition!)

hints.text: Which operation comes first: addition or multiplication?

problems.teachingPoint: PEMDAS: Multiplication comes before addition. 3 + 4 × 2 = 3 + 8 = 11, NOT 7 × 2 = 14.

problems.statement: What is (3 + 4) × 2?

hints.text: Parentheses override the usual order — do them first.

problems.teachingPoint: Parentheses always come first in PEMDAS. They override the normal order. Compare: 3 + 4 × 2 = 11 but (3 + 4) × 2 = 14.

problems.statement: What is 20 - 3 × 4 + 1?

hints.text: Do multiplication first, then work left to right for addition/subtraction.

problems.teachingPoint: After handling multiplication, work left to right for addition and subtraction. They have equal priority.

levels.name: Expression Comparison
levels.storyContext: Lizzie challenges: "Can you compare these expressions WITHOUT plugging in every value?"

problems.statement: For any positive number n, which is greater: 2(n + 3) or 2n + 3? A) 2(n+3) B) 2n+3 C) They are always equal

correctAnswer.displayValue: A — 2(n+3) = 2n + 6 which is always 3 more than 2n + 3

hints.text: Try expanding 2(n + 3) using the distributive property.
2n + 6 vs 2n + 3: the first is always 3 more. So 2(n+3) > 2n + 3.

problems.teachingPoint: Expand using the distributive property: 2(n+3) = 2n+6. Since 2n+6 > 2n+3 always, 2(n+3) is always greater.

problems.statement: If n = 5, which is greater: n² or 2n? (n² means n × n) A) n² B) 2n C) They are equal

correctAnswer.displayValue: A — 5² = 25 and 2(5) = 10, so n² is greater

hints.text: 25 > 10, so n² is greater when n = 5.

problems.teachingPoint: n² grows much faster than 2n for large n. At n = 5: n² = 25 but 2n = 10. Squaring a number makes it much larger than doubling.

problems.statement: For any number n, are 3(n - 2) and 3n - 6 always equal? A) Yes, always B) No, only sometimes C) Never equal

correctAnswer.displayValue: A — By the distributive property, 3(n-2) = 3n - 6 always

hints.text: Try expanding 3(n - 2) using the distributive property.
3(n-2) = 3n - 6. They are always equal — they are the same expression written differently!

problems.solutionExplanation: 3(n-2) = 3n - 6 by the distributive property. Always equal.
problems.teachingPoint: The distributive property shows that a(b - c) = ab - ac. So 3(n-2) and 3n-6 are equivalent expressions — always equal for every value of n.

levels.name: Solving Addition Equations
levels.storyContext: Prof. Owlbert introduces equations. "An equation says two things are equal. To solve it, we isolate the variable!"

problems.statement: Solve: x + 7 = 12. What is x?

hints.text: To isolate x, undo the addition by subtracting.

problems.teachingPoint: To solve addition equations, subtract the same number from both sides. x + 7 = 12 → x = 12 - 7 = 5.

problems.statement: Solve: n + 15 = 23. What is n?

hints.text: Undo addition by subtracting 15 from both sides.

problems.teachingPoint: The inverse of adding 15 is subtracting 15. Always check your answer by substituting back into the original equation.

problems.statement: Solve: y - 9 = 4. What is y?

hints.text: To undo subtraction, add 9 to both sides.

problems.teachingPoint: The inverse of subtracting 9 is adding 9. y - 9 = 4 → y = 4 + 9 = 13.

levels.name: Solving All One-Step
levels.storyContext: Lizzie expands the toolkit. "Addition, subtraction, multiplication, AND division equations — we can solve them all!"

problems.statement: Solve: 5x = 35. What is x?

hints.text: 5x means 5 times x. Undo multiplication by dividing.

problems.teachingPoint: To solve multiplication equations, divide both sides by the coefficient. 5x = 35 → x = 35/5 = 7.

problems.statement: Solve: n ÷ 4 = 9. What is n?

hints.text: n divided by 4 equals 9. Undo division by multiplying.

problems.teachingPoint: To solve division equations, multiply both sides by the divisor. n/4 = 9 → n = 9 × 4 = 36.

problems.statement: Solve: 8x = 72. What is x?

hints.text: Divide both sides by 8 to isolate x.

problems.teachingPoint: Inverse operations: addition↔subtraction, multiplication↔division. Always use the opposite operation to solve.

levels.name: Equation Practice
levels.storyContext: Grogg practices solving equations of all types. "Let me check my answers by plugging back in!"

problems.statement: Solve: x - 14 = 20. What is x?

hints.text: Undo subtraction by adding 14 to both sides.

problems.teachingPoint: Always check your answer by substituting back. 34 - 14 = 20. It works!

problems.statement: Solve: 6n = 54. What is n?
problems.teachingPoint: Solving 6n = 54: divide by 6 to get n = 9. The coefficient 6 is "undone" by dividing.

problems.statement: Solve: m ÷ 7 = 8. What is m?

hints.text: Undo division by multiplying both sides by 7.

problems.teachingPoint: Multiply both sides by 7 to undo the division: m/7 = 8 → m = 56.

levels.name: From Words to Equations
levels.storyContext: Prof. Owlbert explains: "The hardest part of algebra is translating words into equations. Let's practice that bridge."

problems.statement: "A number plus 12 equals 30." Solve for the number.
problems.teachingPoint: Translate step by step: "a number" = n, "plus 12" = + 12, "equals 30" = = 30. Then solve the equation.

problems.statement: "Three times a number equals 45." Solve for the number.
problems.teachingPoint: "Times" means multiplication. "Three times a number equals 45" → 3n = 45 → n = 15.

problems.statement: "A baker makes cookies in batches of 8. After selling some, she has 24 cookies left. How many batches are left?"

hints.text: Let b = number of batches. Each batch has 8 cookies.

problems.teachingPoint: Real-world problems require choosing what the variable represents, writing the equation, then solving. Here b = batches, 8b = 24, b = 3.

levels.name: Grogg's Equation Blunders
levels.storyContext: Grogg shows his equation-solving work. "Check my answers! I think I got them all right." Did he?

problems.statement: Grogg solves x + 9 = 15 and gets x = 24. He added 9 to both sides. What should x be? A) 24 B) 6 C) -6 D) 135

correctAnswer.displayValue: B — To solve x + 9 = 15, subtract 9 from both sides: x = 6

hints.text: What is the inverse of adding 9? Grogg used the wrong operation.
He should subtract 9, not add 9. x = 15 - 9.
x = 15 - 9 = 6. Grogg added instead of subtracting.

problems.solutionExplanation: x = 15 - 9 = 6. Grogg added instead of subtracting.
problems.teachingPoint: To undo addition, SUBTRACT from both sides. Adding to both sides would move farther from the answer.

problems.statement: Grogg solves 4x = 28 by subtracting 4: "x = 28 - 4 = 24." What should x be? A) 24 B) 7 C) 32 D) 112

hints.text: 4x means 4 TIMES x. What undoes multiplication?
Division undoes multiplication. Divide both sides by 4.
x = 28 ÷ 4 = 7. Grogg subtracted instead of dividing.

problems.solutionExplanation: x = 28 ÷ 4 = 7. Grogg used subtraction instead of division.
problems.teachingPoint: Match the inverse operation to the equation type. 4x = 28 uses multiplication, so divide to solve: x = 7.

problems.statement: Grogg translates "5 less than a number is 20" as 5 - n = 20. What is the correct equation and answer? A) 5-n=20, n=-15 B) n-5=20, n=25 C) n+5=20, n=15 D) 5n=20, n=4

correctAnswer.displayValue: B — "5 less than a number" means n - 5, not 5 - n

hints.text: "5 less than a number" — which comes first, the number or the 5?
"Less than" means subtract FROM the number: n - 5, not 5 - n.
n - 5 = 20, so n = 25. Grogg reversed the subtraction order.

problems.solutionExplanation: n - 5 = 20, n = 25. "5 less than n" = n - 5, not 5 - n.
problems.teachingPoint: "5 less than n" means n - 5. The "less than" phrase reverses the order in English vs math. This is one of the most common algebra mistakes!

levels.name: Inequalities
levels.storyContext: Lizzie introduces a new symbol. "Not everything is equal! Sometimes we need < and > for ranges of values."

problems.statement: If x + 3 > 10, which values of x work? A) x = 6 B) x = 7 C) x = 8 D) Both B and C

correctAnswer.displayValue: C — x + 3 > 10 means x > 7. Only x = 8 is greater than 7.

hints.text: Solve x + 3 > 10 by subtracting 3 from both sides.
x > 7 means x must be greater than 7 (not equal to 7).
x > 7: x = 6 gives 9 (no), x = 7 gives 10 (not >), x = 8 gives 11 (yes). Only C works.

problems.teachingPoint: An inequality like x + 3 > 10 means x > 7. The solution is all numbers greater than 7 (not including 7 itself).

problems.statement: Solve: 2n < 16. Which describes ALL solutions? A) n < 8 B) n < 14 C) n > 8 D) n = 8

correctAnswer.displayValue: A — Divide both sides by 2: n < 8

hints.text: Solve like an equation: divide both sides by 2.
n < 8 means any number less than 8 works (like 7, 5, 0, -3...).

problems.teachingPoint: Solve inequalities the same way as equations. Divide both sides by 2: 2n < 16 → n < 8. The inequality sign stays the same when dividing by a positive number.

problems.statement: Write the inequality: "A number n is at least 5." Use ≥ or >= for "at least."

correctAnswer.displayValue: n ≥ 5 means n is 5 or greater

hints.text: "At least" translates to ≥ (greater than or equal to).
"n is at least 5" means n ≥ 5 (or n >= 5).

problems.solutionExplanation: n >= 5 (n is greater than or equal to 5)
problems.teachingPoint: "At least" means ≥ (greater than or equal to). "At most" means ≤ (less than or equal to). These include the boundary value.

levels.name: Equation Puzzles
levels.storyContext: Admiral Axiom speaks in riddles. "I'm thinking of a number... Can you figure it out from my clues?"

problems.statement: "I think of a number, double it, then add 3, and get 19." What is the number?
problems.teachingPoint: For two-step equations, undo operations in reverse order: undo addition first, then undo multiplication.

problems.statement: "I think of a number, subtract 7, then multiply by 3, and get 18." What is the number?

hints.text: First divide by 3: n - 7 = 6. Then add 7.

problems.teachingPoint: Work backwards through the operations: undo the last operation (multiply) first, then undo the first (subtract). Reverse order!

problems.statement: "I think of a number, add 5, then divide by 2, and get 9." What is the number?

hints.text: First multiply by 2: n + 5 = 18. Then subtract 5.

problems.teachingPoint: Multi-step equations: undo operations in reverse order. Last operation done → first to undo.

levels.name: Guardian of Expression Expanse
levels.storyContext: The Guardian of Expression Expanse appears! "Expressions, equations, AND inequalities — show me you have mastered them all!"

problems.statement: If 4(x + 2) = 36, what is x?

hints.text: First divide both sides by 4, then solve for x.

problems.teachingPoint: For equations with parentheses, you can either distribute first or divide first. Here dividing by 4 first is simpler.

problems.statement: Evaluate: 3 × (8 - 2)² ÷ 6 + 1. (Remember: parentheses, then exponents, then multiply/divide, then add.)

hints.text: Follow PEMDAS strictly: Parentheses first, then exponents.

problems.teachingPoint: PEMDAS in action: (8-2)=6, then 6²=36, then left-to-right for ×÷: 3×36÷6=18, finally +1=19.

problems.statement: "I think of a number, multiply by 5, subtract 8, and get 32." What is the number?

hints.text: Add 8 to both sides: 5n = 40. Then divide by 5.

problems.teachingPoint: Two-step equation solving: undo the subtraction first (add 8), then undo the multiplication (divide by 5). Always undo in reverse order.

learningObjectives: Use variables to represent unknown numbers
Write algebraic expressions from word descriptions
Evaluate expressions using order of operations (PEMDAS)
Solve one-step equations with all four operations
Translate word problems into equations and solve
Write and interpret basic inequalities

chapters.name: Statistics Strait

levels.name: The Average Island
levels.storyContext: Prof. Owlbert arrives at Statistics Strait. "The mean — or average — is what each person would get if you shared everything equally."

problems.statement: Find the mean of 4, 8, and 6. (Mean = sum ÷ count)

hints.text: Add all the numbers, then divide by how many there are.

problems.teachingPoint: The mean (average) is the sum of all values divided by the count. It tells you the "fair share" if everything were split evenly.

problems.statement: Five friends scored 10, 8, 6, 9, and 7 on a quiz. What is the mean score?

hints.text: Add all five scores, then divide by 5.

problems.teachingPoint: If all five friends scored 8, the total would be the same (40). The mean "evens out" the differences.

problems.statement: The mean of four numbers is 10. What is their sum?

hints.text: Mean = sum ÷ count. You can rearrange: sum = mean × count.

problems.teachingPoint: Mean = sum/count, so sum = mean × count. If you know the average and how many values, you can find the total.

levels.name: Mean Practice
levels.storyContext: Grogg practices calculating means. "Sum divided by count — I can do this!"

problems.statement: Find the mean of 12, 18, 15, and 11.

hints.text: Add all four numbers, then divide by 4.

problems.teachingPoint: The mean of 12, 18, 15, 11 is 14. Notice it falls between the smallest and largest values.

problems.statement: A student scored 85, 90, 78, and 95 on four tests. What is the mean score?

hints.text: Add the four test scores, divide by 4.

problems.teachingPoint: The mean score is 87. It is pulled down slightly by the lowest score (78) and up by the highest (95).

problems.statement: The mean of 5 numbers is 12. Four of the numbers are 10, 14, 11, and 15. What is the fifth number?

hints.text: If the mean is 12 and there are 5 numbers, what must the total sum be?
Sum = 12 × 5 = 60. The four known numbers sum to 50.

problems.teachingPoint: To find a missing value given the mean: calculate the required sum (mean × count), then subtract the known values.

levels.name: The Middle Value
levels.storyContext: Lizzie explains: "The median is the middle value when you line up all the numbers in order."

problems.statement: Find the median of 3, 7, 5, 9, 1. (First put them in order!)

hints.text: Sort the numbers from least to greatest first.
Ordered: 1, 3, 5, 7, 9. The middle number is the third one.
The median is 5 — it is in the exact middle of the sorted list.

problems.teachingPoint: The median is the middle value after sorting. For an odd number of values, the median is the one in the center position.

problems.statement: Find the median of 4, 8, 2, 10. (Even number of values — average the two middle ones.)

hints.text: Sort: 2, 4, 8, 10. With 4 numbers, there is no single middle — average the middle two.
Middle two are 4 and 8. Average them.

problems.teachingPoint: With an even number of values, the median is the average of the two middle values. Here: (4+8)/2 = 6.

problems.statement: Find the median of 15, 20, 10, 25, 30, 5, 35.

hints.text: Sort the 7 numbers and find the 4th one (middle of 7).
The 4th value is 20. The median is 20.

problems.teachingPoint: For n values, the median is at position (n+1)/2. For 7 values: position 4. The median is 20.

levels.name: Mode and Range
levels.storyContext: Prof. Owlbert adds two more tools. "The mode is the most frequent value. The range shows how spread out the data is."

problems.statement: Find the mode of: 3, 5, 7, 5, 2, 5, 8. The mode is the value that appears most often.

correctAnswer.displayValue: 5 appears 3 times, more than any other value

hints.text: Count how many times each number appears.

problems.teachingPoint: The mode is the value that occurs most frequently. A data set can have one mode, multiple modes, or no mode (if all values appear equally).

problems.statement: Find the range of: 12, 5, 8, 20, 3. (Range = highest - lowest)

hints.text: The range is the difference between the highest and lowest values.

problems.teachingPoint: The range measures how spread out the data is. Range = maximum - minimum. A large range means the data is spread out.

problems.statement: Dataset: 4, 4, 7, 7, 7, 10. What is the mode? A) 4 B) 7 C) 10 D) No mode

correctAnswer.displayValue: B — 7 appears 3 times, more than any other value

hints.text: Count each value: how many 4s, 7s, and 10s?
4 appears twice, 7 appears three times, 10 appears once.

problems.teachingPoint: Even when multiple values repeat, the mode is the one that repeats the MOST. 7 appears 3 times, beating 4 (which appears twice).

levels.name: Mean vs Median
levels.storyContext: Lizzie asks: "When the mean and median give different answers, which one should you use?"

problems.statement: Data: 2, 3, 4, 5, 36. What is the mean?

hints.text: Add all values and divide by 5.

problems.teachingPoint: The mean of 2,3,4,5,36 is 10. Notice that 10 is higher than 4 of the 5 values! The outlier 36 pulls the mean up.

problems.statement: Data: 2, 3, 4, 5, 36. What is the median?

hints.text: Data is already sorted. Find the middle value of 5 numbers.
The 3rd value (middle of 5) is the median.

problems.teachingPoint: The median (4) better represents this data than the mean (10) because the outlier 36 does not affect the median.

problems.statement: A set of salaries: $30K, $35K, $40K, $45K, $500K. Which measure best represents the "typical" salary? A) Mean B) Median

correctAnswer.displayValue: B — The median ($40K) is typical; the mean ($130K) is skewed by the $500K outlier

hints.text: The mean is pulled by extreme values. Is there an extreme value here?
$500K is much higher than the rest. It will inflate the mean.
Median = $40K (typical). Mean ≈ $130K (inflated by the outlier). Median is more representative.

problems.solutionExplanation: Median ($40K) — not affected by the $500K outlier.
problems.teachingPoint: When data has outliers (extreme values), the median is more representative than the mean. The median resists the pull of outliers.

levels.name: Reading Bar Graphs
levels.storyContext: Grogg finds a bar graph on a sign. "Each bar shows how many — taller bars mean more!"

problems.statement: A bar graph shows: Red=8, Blue=12, Green=6, Yellow=10. How many total items are there?

hints.text: Add up all the bar values to find the total.

problems.teachingPoint: To find the total from a bar graph, add up the values represented by each bar.

problems.statement: In the same graph (Red=8, Blue=12, Green=6, Yellow=10), how many more items are Blue than Green?

hints.text: Subtract the smaller from the larger to find the difference.

problems.teachingPoint: To compare categories in a bar graph, subtract the smaller value from the larger.

problems.statement: Red=8, Blue=12, Green=6, Yellow=10. What is the mean number of items per color?
problems.teachingPoint: You can compute statistics from graph data just like from a list of numbers. The mean is the total divided by the number of categories.

levels.name: Histograms and Line Plots
levels.storyContext: Prof. Owlbert shows different types of graphs. "Histograms group data into ranges. Line plots show individual data points."

problems.statement: A histogram shows: 0-10: 5 students, 11-20: 12 students, 21-30: 3 students. How many students total? A) 17 B) 20 C) 15 D) 30

hints.text: Add the frequencies from each bar/bin.

problems.teachingPoint: Histograms group data into bins (ranges). The height of each bar shows how many data points fall in that range.

problems.statement: Which is better for showing exact individual values: a histogram or a line plot? A) Histogram B) Line plot

correctAnswer.displayValue: B — Line plots show each individual data point

hints.text: Histograms group data into ranges. Line plots show each value.
If you want to see exact values, you need individual points.
Line plots show every individual value, while histograms group them. Line plots are better for exact values.

problems.solutionExplanation: Line plots show individual data points.
problems.teachingPoint: Line plots (dot plots) show each data point individually. Histograms group data into bins — you lose individual values but see the overall shape.

problems.statement: A line plot shows test scores: 70 (2 dots), 80 (5 dots), 90 (3 dots). What is the total number of students?

hints.text: Each dot represents one student. Count all dots.

problems.teachingPoint: In a line plot, each dot represents one data point. The total number of data points is the sum of all dots.

levels.name: Choosing the Right Display
levels.storyContext: Lizzie has different datasets. "Not every graph works for every type of data. Let's match them!"

problems.statement: You want to show favorite ice cream flavors among 30 students. Best display? A) Line plot B) Bar graph C) Histogram D) Scatter plot

correctAnswer.displayValue: B — Bar graphs are best for comparing categories (flavors)

hints.text: Ice cream flavors are categories, not numbers on a scale.
For categorical data, you need a graph that shows counts per category.
Bar graphs compare categories. Each flavor gets its own bar.

problems.solutionExplanation: Bar graph — best for comparing categorical data.
problems.teachingPoint: Bar graphs are ideal for categorical data (flavors, colors, types). Histograms are for numerical ranges.

problems.statement: You want to show the distribution of 100 test scores (0-100). Best display? A) Bar graph B) Pie chart C) Histogram D) Line plot

correctAnswer.displayValue: C — Histograms group numerical data into ranges, perfect for showing score distributions

hints.text: Test scores are numerical. You want to see the shape of the distribution.
With 100 different possible scores, individual bars would be too many. Grouping into ranges helps.
Histograms group numerical data into bins (like 0-10, 11-20, etc.) showing the distribution shape.

problems.solutionExplanation: Histogram — groups numerical data into bins.
problems.teachingPoint: Histograms are perfect for showing how numerical data is distributed. They group values into bins and show the frequency of each bin.

problems.statement: You have 15 students' exact heights. You want to see each individual value. Best display? A) Histogram B) Bar graph C) Line plot D) Pie chart

correctAnswer.displayValue: C — Line plots (dot plots) show each individual data point

hints.text: You want to see EACH individual value, not grouped data.
With only 15 values, you can show each one as a dot.
A line plot (dot plot) shows each data point individually on a number line.

problems.solutionExplanation: Line plot — shows each individual value.
problems.teachingPoint: Line plots (dot plots) are great for small datasets where you want to see every individual value. For large datasets, use histograms.

levels.name: Misleading Statistics
levels.storyContext: Admiral Axiom warns: "Not all statistics tell the truth. Some graphs and numbers are designed to mislead you!"

problems.statement: A graph shows sales going from 100 to 110, but the y-axis starts at 95 instead of 0. This makes the increase look: A) Smaller than it really is B) Larger than it really is C) About right D) Impossible to tell

correctAnswer.value: B) Larger than it really is
correctAnswer.displayValue: B — Starting the y-axis above zero exaggerates the visual difference between bars

hints.text: When the y-axis doesn't start at zero, what happens to the visual comparison?
The bar for 110 looks much taller than 100 when the axis starts at 95 vs starting at 0.
A truncated y-axis makes a 10% increase look like a 200-300% increase visually. It exaggerates.

problems.teachingPoint: A y-axis that doesn't start at zero makes differences look bigger than they are. Always check the axis scale!

problems.statement: A company says "Customer satisfaction is at 95%!" but they only surveyed 20 of their most loyal customers. Is this misleading? A) No, 95% is clearly good B) Yes, the sample is biased

correctAnswer.value: B) Yes, the sample is biased
correctAnswer.displayValue: B — Only surveying loyal customers creates a biased sample that overestimates satisfaction

hints.text: Would loyal customers be more or less satisfied than average?
A sample should represent ALL customers, not just the most loyal ones.
Sampling only loyal customers gives artificially high results. The sample is biased.

problems.solutionExplanation: Biased sample — only loyal customers surveyed.
problems.teachingPoint: A biased sample does not represent the whole population. Survey results are only valid if the sample is randomly selected and representative.

problems.statement: "The average salary at XYZ Corp is $200,000!" If the CEO makes $5,000,000 and 49 employees make $100,000, is the mean misleading here? A) No, it is accurate B) Yes, the median would be better

correctAnswer.value: B) Yes, the median would be better
correctAnswer.displayValue: B — One extreme salary pulls the mean far above what most employees earn

hints.text: Is $200K representative of what most people at the company earn?
The CEO salary is an extreme outlier that pulls the mean way up.
Mean = ($5M + 49×$100K)/50 = $198K. But 49 of 50 earn $100K. Median = $100K is more representative.

problems.solutionExplanation: Median ($100K) better represents typical salary than mean ($198K).
problems.teachingPoint: When a dataset has extreme outliers, the mean can be misleading. The median gives a better picture of what is "typical."

levels.name: Surveys and Sampling
levels.storyContext: Prof. Owlbert explains: "To learn about a large group, we study a smaller sample. But the sample must be fair!"

problems.statement: To find out what music students at a school prefer, which sample is best? A) Ask the band class B) Ask every 5th student entering school C) Ask your friends D) Ask the teachers

correctAnswer.value: B) Ask every 5th student entering school
correctAnswer.displayValue: B — Systematic sampling from all students is the least biased method

hints.text: Which group best represents ALL students at the school?
Band students like music. Friends are similar to you. Teachers are not students.
Every 5th student is random and includes students from all groups. This is least biased.

problems.teachingPoint: A good sample is random and representative. Asking every 5th student captures variety. Asking only one group (band, friends) creates bias.

problems.statement: A survey of 10 people finds 7 prefer dogs. Can we conclude that 70% of the entire country prefers dogs? A) Yes, 70% is clear B) No, the sample is too small

correctAnswer.value: B) No, the sample is too small
correctAnswer.displayValue: B — 10 people is far too small to represent an entire country

hints.text: How well can 10 people represent millions?
Small samples have high variability — results could be very different with a different 10 people.
A sample of 10 is too small to generalize to a whole country. Larger samples give more reliable results.

problems.teachingPoint: Larger samples give more reliable results. A sample of 10 people cannot accurately represent millions. Statistical claims need adequate sample sizes.

problems.statement: A survey question asks: "Don't you agree that our park is wonderful?" Is this a good survey question? A) Yes, it is clear B) No, it is biased/leading

correctAnswer.displayValue: B — The question leads the respondent toward agreeing

hints.text: Does the question suggest what answer the surveyor wants?
"Don't you agree" pushes toward "yes." A neutral question would not suggest an answer.
Leading questions bias the results. A better question: "How would you rate our park?"

problems.teachingPoint: Good survey questions are neutral and do not suggest an answer. "Don't you agree..." is a leading question that biases results.

levels.name: Data Detective
levels.storyContext: Lizzie challenges: "Given the mean, median, and mode — can you figure out the missing data?"

problems.statement: A set of 5 numbers has a mean of 8 and a median of 7. The numbers in order are: 3, 5, 7, ?, 15. What is the missing number?

hints.text: Use the mean to find the total sum.

problems.teachingPoint: When you know the mean and count, you can find the total sum. Then subtract the known values to find the missing one.

problems.statement: Three numbers have a mean of 12 and a range of 10. The smallest number is 7. What is the largest number?

hints.text: Range = largest - smallest. You know the range and smallest.
Largest = 17. Sum = 36. Third = 36-7-17 = 12. Check: mean = 36/3 = 12. Correct!

problems.teachingPoint: Range = max - min. If you know the range and minimum, add them to find the maximum.

problems.statement: A student has test scores of 85, 92, and 78. What score does she need on a 4th test to have a mean of 88?

hints.text: Figure out what total sum of 4 tests gives a mean of 88.

problems.teachingPoint: To reach a target mean: compute required total (mean × count), subtract what you already have. This is a very practical skill for grades!

levels.name: Statistics Puzzles
levels.storyContext: Admiral Axiom presents tricky statistics problems. "Think carefully about what the numbers really tell you!"

problems.statement: Adding the number 20 to a set increases the mean from 10 to 12. How many numbers were in the set originally?

correctAnswer.displayValue: Old sum = 10n. New sum = 10n+20. New mean = (10n+20)/(n+1)=12. Solve: 10n+20=12n+12, 8=2n, n=4

hints.text: Let n = original count. Old sum = 10n. New sum = 10n + 20. New count = n + 1.

problems.teachingPoint: Algebra meets statistics! Set up an equation using the mean formula and solve for the unknown count.

problems.statement: In a class of 20 students, the mean score is 75. If the top 5 scores are removed, the mean of the remaining 15 drops to 70. What was the mean of the removed 5 scores?

hints.text: Find the total for all 20, then the total for 15. The difference is the removed total.

problems.teachingPoint: You can work with sub-groups by computing their totals from means and counts, then finding differences.

problems.statement: Five numbers have mode 7, median 7, and mean 8. The largest number is 15. The numbers in order are: ?, 7, 7, ?, 15. Find the first number.

correctAnswer.displayValue: Sum=40. Known: 7+7+15=29. Missing two sum=11. First must be ≤7 for median. If 4th is x: 4+x=11. x must be ≥7. x=7,first=4

hints.text: Sum = 5 × 8 = 40. Two 7s and 15 give 29. The other two sum to 11.
The 4th number must be ≥ 7 (for sorted order). The 1st must be ≤ 7.
If 4th = 7 (supports mode), then 1st = 11-7 = 4. Check: 4,7,7,7,15. Mode=7, median=7, mean=8. Works!

problems.teachingPoint: Combining mode, median, and mean constraints narrows down the possibilities. Use each constraint to eliminate options.

levels.name: Guardian of Statistics Strait
levels.storyContext: The Guardian of Statistics Strait demands proof of your mastery! "Mean, median, mode — and do not be fooled by misleading data!"

problems.statement: Dataset: 5, 8, 8, 10, 12, 14, 20. Find the mean.

hints.text: Add all 7 values, then divide by 7.

problems.teachingPoint: The mean of 5,8,8,10,12,14,20 is 11. Add all values and divide by the count.

problems.statement: Same dataset: 5, 8, 8, 10, 12, 14, 20. What is the median?

hints.text: Data is sorted. Find the middle value of 7 numbers.
The 4th value (middle of 7) is the median.

problems.teachingPoint: The median (10) and mean (11) differ slightly because the data is slightly right-skewed (20 pulls the mean up).

problems.statement: A student needs a mean of 90 across 5 tests. She scored 88, 92, 85, and 91 on the first four. What must she score on test 5?

hints.text: What total score across 5 tests gives a mean of 90?

problems.teachingPoint: To reach a target mean: total required = mean × count. Then subtract what you have. This is one of the most useful statistics skills!

learningObjectives: Calculate mean, median, mode, and range
Choose between mean and median based on data distribution
Read and interpret bar graphs, histograms, and line plots
Identify misleading statistics and biased samples
Solve problems requiring working backwards from statistics

chapters.name: Factor Fjords

levels.name: Divisibility Dock
levels.storyContext: Prof. Owlbert greets you at Factor Fjords. "Divisibility rules are shortcuts that tell you if one number divides evenly into another."

problems.statement: Is 248 divisible by 2? A) Yes B) No

correctAnswer.displayValue: A — 248 ends in 8, which is even, so it is divisible by 2

hints.text: A number is divisible by 2 if it is even (ends in 0, 2, 4, 6, or 8).
8 is even, so 248 is divisible by 2.

problems.teachingPoint: Divisibility by 2: check if the last digit is even (0, 2, 4, 6, or 8). This is the simplest divisibility rule.

problems.statement: Is 735 divisible by 5? A) Yes B) No

correctAnswer.displayValue: A — 735 ends in 5, so it is divisible by 5

hints.text: Divisibility by 5: the last digit must be 0 or 5.
Since 735 ends in 5, it is divisible by 5. 735 ÷ 5 = 147.

problems.teachingPoint: Divisibility by 5: the number must end in 0 or 5. Divisibility by 10: must end in 0.

problems.statement: Is 4,530 divisible by 10? A) Yes B) No

correctAnswer.displayValue: A — 4,530 ends in 0, so it is divisible by 10

hints.text: Divisibility by 10: the number must end in 0.

problems.teachingPoint: If a number ends in 0, it is divisible by both 5 and 10. The last digit tells you a lot about divisibility!

levels.name: More Divisibility Rules
levels.storyContext: Lizzie teaches the trickier rules. "For 3 and 9, add up the digits. For 4, check the last two digits."

problems.statement: Is 357 divisible by 3? (Add the digits: 3+5+7=15. Is 15 divisible by 3?) A) Yes B) No

correctAnswer.displayValue: A — Digit sum = 15, and 15 ÷ 3 = 5, so 357 is divisible by 3

hints.text: Divisibility by 3: add all digits. If the sum is divisible by 3, so is the number.

problems.solutionExplanation: Yes — digit sum 15 is divisible by 3.
problems.teachingPoint: Divisibility by 3: sum the digits. If the sum is divisible by 3, so is the original number. This works because of place value properties!

problems.statement: Is 516 divisible by 4? (Check: are the last two digits "16" divisible by 4?) A) Yes B) No

correctAnswer.displayValue: A — The last two digits are 16, and 16 ÷ 4 = 4, so 516 is divisible by 4

hints.text: Divisibility by 4: check if the last two digits form a number divisible by 4.
Last two digits: 16. Is 16 ÷ 4 a whole number?

problems.solutionExplanation: Yes — last two digits "16" are divisible by 4.
problems.teachingPoint: Divisibility by 4: check the last two digits only. If they form a number divisible by 4, the whole number is too.

problems.statement: Is 738 divisible by 9? (Digit sum: 7+3+8=18. Is 18 divisible by 9?) A) Yes B) No

correctAnswer.displayValue: A — Digit sum = 18, and 18 ÷ 9 = 2, so 738 is divisible by 9

hints.text: Divisibility by 9: add digits. If the sum is divisible by 9, so is the number.

problems.solutionExplanation: Yes — digit sum 18 is divisible by 9.
problems.teachingPoint: Divisibility by 9: same trick as 3, but the digit sum must be divisible by 9. If divisible by 9, it is also divisible by 3.

levels.name: Divisibility Mastery
levels.storyContext: Grogg tests all the rules. "6 means divisible by BOTH 2 and 3. And there are tricks for 7, 8, and 11 too!"

problems.statement: Is 432 divisible by 6? (Must pass BOTH the 2-test AND the 3-test.) A) Yes B) No

correctAnswer.displayValue: A — 432 is even (divisible by 2) and digit sum=9 (divisible by 3), so divisible by 6

hints.text: Divisible by 6 = divisible by BOTH 2 and 3.
Both tests pass, so 432 is divisible by 6. 432÷6=72.

problems.teachingPoint: Divisibility by 6: the number must be divisible by BOTH 2 and 3. Check both rules!

problems.statement: Is 1,024 divisible by 8? (Check: are the last three digits "024" divisible by 8?) A) Yes B) No

hints.text: Divisibility by 8: check if the last three digits form a number divisible by 8.
Last three digits: 024 = 24. Is 24 ÷ 8 a whole number?
